readerTitle: Signups are up. Why isn't revenue?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당용 근무표 앱, 식자재 유통회사 운영팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 구독 소프트웨어는 신규 가입 수가 아니라 고객이 머무는 기간, 고객과 함께 커지는 가격, 결제 주기라는 세 가지 다이얼로 판단한다.
misconception: 구독 매출이 정체되면 신규 고객을 더 데려오면 된다. 연간 결제는 무조건 싸서 이득이다.

sources.text: 구독 사업의 표준 개념 (해지율, 고객 수 상한, 확장 매출, 순매출 유지율, 연간·월간 결제)

cards.title: Signups are up. Why isn't revenue?
body: Maya sells a shift-scheduling app to restaurants for $40 a month per location. Every month, about 100 new restaurants sign up.
Yet for half a year, monthly revenue has barely moved. Her team wants a bigger ad budget. Today you'll use three ideas from this unit to decide what she should actually do.

image.label: A dashboard with a rising signup line and a flat revenue line
image.brief: 작은 사무실 책상 위 노트북 화면. 대시보드에 "New signups" 선은 꾸준히 오르고 "Monthly revenue" 선은 평평함. 창업자가 턱을 괴고 화면을 봄. 실제 소프트웨어 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where should next quarter's effort go?
body: Maya gets 100 new restaurants a month. About 8% of paying restaurants cancel each month.
She can focus on one thing next quarter. Which?

options.text: Double the ad budget to get 200 signups a month
options.feedback: This works, but only while she keeps paying for it. Under **the math of retention**, the cancellations still eat 8% of the base every month.

options.text: Find out why restaurants cancel and fix the biggest reason
options.feedback: Halving cancellations raises her ceiling as much as doubling signups, without a bigger ad bill every month. That's **the math of retention** at work.

options.text: Cut the price to $30 so more restaurants try it
options.feedback: She'd earn less from every restaurant, including loyal ones, and a cheaper app doesn't fix whatever makes people leave.

cards.title: Every leaky bucket has a ceiling.
body: When new customers equal cancellations, growth stops. That point is new signups ÷ cancellation rate. Maya is already close to it.

breakdown.label: Double signups
breakdown.detail: 200 ÷ 8%, paid for with ads every month

cards.softwareNote: In subscription software, this ceiling is why churn matters more than signups once a product has a steady flow of new users.

cards.title: Most cancellations happened early.
body: Maya called 20 restaurants that had cancelled. Most left in their first two months, before they had built a single full schedule.

So she changed the first week. Her team now sets up the first schedule with the manager on a call. The goal isn't more features. It's getting every new restaurant to the moment the app saves them time.
cards.callout: Retention problems are often onboarding problems.

cards.title: Some customers are opening new locations.
body: A few restaurant groups now use the app across three or four sites. Maya is reviewing her pricing.

options.text: One flat price per restaurant group, however many sites
options.feedback: Simple to sell, but her revenue stays flat while customers get more value. She gives up **expansion revenue** entirely.

options.text: $40 per location, so the price grows as the customer grows
options.feedback: The bill rises only when the customer gets more value. That's **expansion revenue**: more money from the customers you already have.

options.text: Charge per staff member who uses the app
options.feedback: It also grows with customers, but managers may share logins or leave staff out to save money, and that weakens the app.

cards.title: Growth from customers you already have.
body: Take 100 single-site restaurants paying $4,000 a month. Five cancel: −$200. Ten open a second site: +$400.
The same group now pays **$4,200**, or 105% of where it started, with no new signups at all. Expansion can outrun cancellations.

image.label: Bar showing $4,000 shrinking by $200 then growing by $400
image.brief: 폭포형 막대 그래프. "Start $4,000" → "Cancelled −$200"(빨강) → "New locations +$400"(초록) → "End $4,200". 마지막 막대를 강조.

cards.title: Annual plans can hide a problem.
body: Sellers love annual plans: cash up front and fewer chances to cancel. But a customer who stops using the app in month three can't leave until month twelve.
Your cancellation rate looks great, then a wave of non-renewals arrives at once. Watch usage, not just payments.

cards.title: Now you're the buyer, inside a big company.
body: You run the regional operations team at a food distributor. Your team tested route-planning software for two weeks and liked it. The drivers haven't used it yet.
It costs $500 a month, or $5,000 a year paid up front. What do you do?

options.feedback: The saving is real, about 17%. But you lock in $5,000 before knowing if drivers will use it.

options.text: Pay monthly until drivers use it, then switch to annual
options.feedback: You pay a little more for a few months and keep the option to walk away. That's **annual vs monthly**: a discount in exchange for commitment.

options.text: Buy annual plans for every region at once
options.feedback: The biggest discount and the biggest bet. If drivers reject it, every region pays for a tool no one opens.

cards.title: Three dials run every subscription.
body: You used **the math of retention** to see Maya's ceiling, **expansion revenue** to price for growing customers, and **annual vs monthly** to weigh a discount against commitment.
**Try it today:** for one subscription you sell or buy, write down how long customers stay, whether the price grows with them, and who carries the risk of the billing period.
